faq.q: Is the Armenian alphabet hard to learn?
faq.a: Not really — it has 39 letters and, unlike English, each letter almost always makes exactly one sound. Once you've drilled the sounds, reading Armenian is far more predictable than reading English.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn the Armenian alphabet?
faq.a: Most learners can recognize and sound out every letter within one to two weeks of short daily practice — Haylingua's own alphabet course is broken into 11 bite-sized lessons for exactly this pace.

faq.q: What's the difference between Eastern and Western Armenian letters?
faq.a: The letterforms and alphabet order are identical — the difference is in pronunciation of certain letter pairs. Haylingua teaches Standard Eastern Armenian, the form used in Armenia today.

faq.q: Do I need to learn cursive Armenian handwriting?
faq.a: Not to read or type Armenian — the printed letterforms shown on this page are what you'll see everywhere online and in most print. Handwriting is a separate, optional skill you can pick up later.

meta.title: Armenian Pronunciation Guide: How to Pronounce Armenian
meta.description: Learn how to pronounce Armenian correctly with real native audio. Master aspirated vs. unaspirated consonants, both Armenian R sounds, and tricky letters with no English equivalent.

hero.title: Armenian Pronunciation
hero.subtitle: Armenian is almost entirely phonetic — once you know a letter's sound, it's the same in every word. The hard part isn't the rules, it's a handful of sounds English speakers haven't trained their mouths to make. Here's what to listen for, with real audio.

trickyPairs.title: Unaspirated vs. aspirated stops
trickyPairs.text: Armenian distinguishes a plain, no-breath consonant from the same consonant said with a burst of air — a contrast English doesn't make. Compare a crisp «տ» (t) with a puffed-out «թ» (t').

trickyPairs.title: Two kinds of R
trickyPairs.text: Eastern Armenian has a light single tongue-tap «ր» (close to the American 'tt' in 'butter') and a strongly rolled/trilled «ռ» — mixing them up is one of the most common beginner errors.

trickyPairs.title: Sounds with no English equivalent
trickyPairs.text: A few Armenian consonants don't map onto anything in English at all — «խ» is a rasping throat sound like the Scottish 'ch' in loch, and «ղ» is a soft, gargled sound close to a French 'r'.

easternArmenian.note: The two share the same 39-letter alphabet and a large amount of vocabulary and grammar — the biggest practical difference for a beginner is pronunciation, especially of the plain vs. puffed-out consonant pairs (see the {{link}}).

faq.q: Is Eastern or Western Armenian more useful to learn?
faq.a: It depends on who you'll speak with. Eastern Armenian is the official language of the Republic of Armenia and is spoken by the majority of Armenian speakers worldwide. Western Armenian is more common among diaspora communities with roots in the Ottoman Empire — parts of the U.S., France, and the Middle East.

faq.q: Can an Eastern Armenian speaker understand Western Armenian?
faq.a: Largely yes, with practice — the two are close enough that speakers can often follow each other, similar to the relationship between some closely related Romance languages. Vocabulary, some grammar, and especially pronunciation differ enough to cause real confusion at first.

faq.q: Does Haylingua teach Western Armenian too?
faq.a: Not yet — Haylingua's course teaches Standard Eastern Armenian. It's a natural foundation even if your family speaks Western Armenian, since the alphabet and a large share of vocabulary and grammar overlap.

meta.title: Armenian Numbers 1–100: Count in Armenian With Pronunciation
meta.description: Learn Armenian numbers from 1 to 100 with Armenian script and pronunciation for every number, plus how compound numbers and ordinals are built.

hero.title: Armenian Numbers 1–100
hero.subtitle: Every number you need for prices, ages, dates, and phone numbers — in Armenian script, with pronunciation for each one.

armenianNumbers.compoundsNote: Past twenty, Armenian stacks the ten and the ones digit into a single word — no extra connector, no hyphen. Twenty-five is քսանհինգ (k'san-hing), literally "twenty-five" run together. Once you know the ten words above and the digits 1–9, you can build every number up to 99 without learning anything new.
armenianNumbers.ordinalsNote: Ordinals are formed from the cardinal number, mostly with the ending -երորդ (-erord). The first three are irregular and worth memorising as-is; everything from fourth onward follows the pattern.

faq.q: Are Armenian numbers hard to learn?
faq.a: They're one of the easier parts of the language. The digits 1–10 are short, the teens are transparent compounds of "ten" plus the digit, and everything above twenty follows one predictable stacking rule. Most learners are comfortable counting to 100 within a few days.

faq.q: Does Armenian use the same digits as English?
faq.a: Yes — modern Armenian writes numerals with the same 0–9 Arabic digits you already use, so prices, phone numbers, and dates are readable straight away. There is also a historical Armenian numeral system that uses letters of the alphabet, but you'll only meet it in old manuscripts and on monuments, not in everyday life.

faq.q: Are these numbers Eastern or Western Armenian?
faq.a: The words on this page are Standard Eastern Armenian, the form spoken in Armenia today. Western Armenian uses the same number words, but pronounces several consonants differently — for example the initial sounds shift, so the same spelling is voiced differently. See our Western vs Eastern Armenian comparison for the full picture.

faq.q: How do I say a year or a phone number in Armenian?
faq.a: Years are read as a full number (հազար ինը հարյուր… for 19xx), while phone numbers are usually read digit by digit, exactly as in English. Both only require the 0–100 vocabulary on this page plus հազար (ha-zar, thousand).

armenianPhrases.politenessNote: Armenian has a formal and an informal "you", and travelers are safest defaulting to the formal one (դուք, duk') with anyone they haven't been introduced to. The phrases above already use the polite forms, so you can say them to a stranger without a second thought.

faq.q: Do I need Armenian to travel in Armenia?
faq.a: You can get by without it — Russian is widely understood and English is common among younger people and in Yerevan's tourist areas. But even a handful of Armenian phrases changes how people respond to you, especially outside the capital, and it's genuinely appreciated rather than treated as a novelty.

faq.q: Which Armenian should I learn for travel to Armenia?
faq.a: Eastern Armenian. That's what's spoken in Armenia itself, and it's what every phrase on this page uses. Western Armenian is the diaspora variety — invaluable if you're connecting with family in Lebanon, Los Angeles, or Europe, but not what you'll hear in Yerevan.

faq.q: Will people understand me if my pronunciation is imperfect?
faq.a: Almost always, yes. The sounds most likely to trip you up are the aspirated consonants — the difference between a plain and a "puffed" p, t, or k can change a word, but context usually carries you through. Listening to real audio while you learn matters far more than drilling the script silently.

faq.q: Is Armenian written in its own alphabet?
faq.a: Yes — 39 letters, created around 405 AD, unrelated to Latin or Cyrillic. Street signs and menus in Armenia are largely in Armenian script, often alongside English in tourist areas. Learning to read it takes a few days and makes navigating dramatically easier.

meta.title: Western vs Eastern Armenian: Differences & Which to Learn
meta.description: Western and Eastern Armenian compared — where each is spoken, how pronunciation and spelling differ, how mutually intelligible they are, and which one you should learn.

hero.title: Western vs Eastern Armenian
hero.subtitle: Two standard forms of the same language, shaped by very different histories. Here's how they actually differ — and how to decide which one to learn.

westernVsEastern.intro: Armenian split into two written standards in the nineteenth century, along the border between the Ottoman and Russian empires. Eastern Armenian became the language of what is now the Republic of Armenia; Western Armenian became the language of the communities that were scattered across the world after 1915. They share an alphabet, most of their vocabulary, and their grammar's underlying shape — speakers of one can generally follow the other after a short adjustment, the way a Lisbon and a São Paulo speaker manage Portuguese.

comparisonRows.western: The global diaspora — Lebanon, Syria, France, the US, Argentina

comparisonRows.eastern: Several million, with a national state behind it
comparisonRows.western: Fewer, and classified by UNESCO as endangered

comparisonRows.eastern: Official language of the Republic of Armenia
comparisonRows.western: No state; sustained by diaspora schools, churches, and press

comparisonRows.eastern: Present tense built with the participle plus "to be"
comparisonRows.western: Present tense marked with the prefix կը (gə)

comparisonRows.eastern: Travel to Armenia, business, most online resources
comparisonRows.western: Connecting with diaspora family and heritage communities

westernVsEastern.soundShiftHeading: The sound shift, in one rule
westernVsEastern.soundShift: The difference you'll notice first is a consistent swap in how certain consonants are voiced. Where Eastern Armenian says a voiced b, d, or g, Western Armenian typically says an unvoiced p, t, or k — and vice versa. The spelling stays identical; only the pronunciation moves. Once you internalise this single correspondence, a surprising amount of the other variety becomes readable to you immediately.
westernVsEastern.whichToLearnHeading: So which one should you learn?
westernVsEastern.whichToLearnIntro: There's no universally better answer — it depends entirely on why you're learning. In practice:
whichToLearnPoints: Learn **Eastern** if you're travelling to, working with, or moving to Armenia, or if you simply want the variety with the most learning material, media, and everyday online use.
Learn **Western** if your family is from the diaspora and Western Armenian is what your grandparents spoke — that connection is the whole point, and it's the variety at genuine risk of being lost.
If you have no particular tie either way, Eastern is the more practical starting point, and what you learn transfers substantially if you later pick up Western.
westernVsEastern.whatWeTeach: Haylingua teaches Standard Eastern Armenian — the form spoken in Armenia today. If your goal is Western Armenian specifically, we'd rather tell you that plainly up front than have you discover it three lessons in. Much of the alphabet and vocabulary work still transfers, but the pronunciation and verb forms you'll hear here are Eastern.

faq.q: Can Eastern and Western Armenian speakers understand each other?
faq.a: Largely, yes. The two are mutually intelligible for most everyday purposes, though the first conversation takes some adjustment — the consonant shift and a handful of high-frequency verb forms are what cause the initial friction. Written Armenian is easier to cross over than spoken, since the alphabet is shared.

faq.q: Do they use the same alphabet?
faq.a: Yes, the same 39-letter Armenian alphabet. The difference is spelling convention: Eastern Armenian adopted a spelling reform in the Soviet period, while Western Armenian kept the classical orthography. Some words are therefore spelled differently even though the letters are identical.

faq.q: Which one is 'real' or 'original' Armenian?
faq.a: Neither, and it's worth pushing back on the premise. Both descend from Classical Armenian (Grabar) and both are legitimate modern standards with their own literature. Western Armenian preserves the older spelling; Eastern Armenian has the larger living speaker base. Neither is a corruption of the other.

faq.q: Is Western Armenian dying out?
faq.a: It's genuinely endangered — UNESCO classifies it as such — because it has no state backing it and is transmitted mainly through diaspora families and schools. That's precisely why heritage learners choosing Western Armenian are doing something valuable, even though it's the harder path for finding resources.

meta.title: How to Choose an Armenian Learning App (2026 Guide)
meta.description: What actually matters when picking an app to learn Armenian — alphabet coverage, real audio, Eastern vs Western, and the questions worth asking before you commit.

hero.title: How to choose an Armenian learning app
hero.subtitle: Armenian is served by far fewer tools than Spanish or French, and the ones that exist differ in ways that matter. Here's what to check before you commit your time.

choosingAnApp.disclosure: Straight up: Haylingua is our own app, so treat this as an informed argument rather than a neutral review. We've written the criteria below to be useful even if you decide something else fits you better — and we'll tell you plainly where we're not the right answer.

criteria.title: Does it teach the alphabet properly?
criteria.text: Armenian has its own 39-letter script, unrelated to Latin or Cyrillic. An app that transliterates everything into Latin letters lets you start faster but leaves you unable to read a menu, a street sign, or a message from a relative. Check that the script is taught from the first lesson, not bolted on later as an optional extra.

criteria.title: Is there real audio on every word?
criteria.text: Armenian distinguishes plain from aspirated consonants — the difference between a plain and a "puffed" p, t, or k is meaningful, and it's nearly impossible to acquire from text alone. A handful of sample recordings isn't enough. You want audio attached to every item you're asked to learn.

criteria.title: Eastern or Western Armenian?
criteria.text: This is the single most consequential question, and many tools don't state it clearly. Eastern is spoken in Armenia; Western is the diaspora variety. Learning the wrong one for your goal is a genuinely costly mistake, so find the answer before your first lesson — see our full comparison if you're unsure which you want.

criteria.title: Was it built for Armenian, or ported to it?
criteria.text: Apps that cover dozens of languages from one template tend to treat Armenian's specifics — its sound system, its script, its verb formation — as an afterthought. A tool built for Armenian alone can structure the whole curriculum around the things that actually make it hard.

criteria.title: Can you actually sustain it?
criteria.text: The best app is the one you still open in week six. Short lessons, a visible streak, and immediate feedback matter more than an exhaustive syllabus you abandon. Be honest about whether a tool fits ten minutes on a commute or assumes an hour at a desk.

criteria.title: What does it cost to find out?
criteria.text: Armenian tools vary from free to subscription-only. A meaningful free tier lets you get through the alphabet and judge the teaching quality before paying for anything — which is the only reliable way to evaluate any of this.

faq.q: Is Armenian on Duolingo?
faq.a: No — Duolingo has never offered an Armenian course, and it remains one of the most commonly searched disappointments for new Armenian learners. If you arrived here after searching for it, you'll need to look at Armenian-specific or smaller multi-language tools instead.

faq.q: Can I learn Armenian free?
faq.a: Yes, at least to a real foundation. Haylingua is free to start with no card required, and there are also free community resources, YouTube channels, and Anki decks. Paid tutoring becomes genuinely valuable later, once you have enough language to make conversation practice worthwhile.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn Armenian?
faq.a: The alphabet takes most learners under a week. Basic conversational footing — greetings, numbers, ordering, simple questions — is a matter of a few months of consistent short sessions. Fluency, as with any language, is measured in years, and depends far more on regular contact with the language than on which app you picked.

faq.q: Is Armenian hard for English speakers?
faq.a: It's moderately hard: a new script, a case system, and some unfamiliar consonant distinctions. But the script is phonetic and learnable in days, and Armenian spelling is far more consistent than English. The difficulty is mostly front-loaded, which is why the first two weeks matter so much.

intro.heading: Type Armenian on any computer
intro.body: Armenian has its own 39-letter alphabet, and most people learning it are sitting at a keyboard printed with Latin letters. That's the real obstacle — not the script itself, but never knowing where the letters live. This trainer teaches the Armenian keyboard the way a touch-typing course does: one finger pair at a time, starting from the home row, with the next key and the finger that presses it shown on screen until you no longer need to look.

setup.heading: Adding the Armenian keyboard to your computer
setup.body: You don't need one to start — the on-screen keyboard here works on its own. But once the layout feels familiar, switching your system input is what makes it usable everywhere else.
macSteps: Next to Input Sources, click Edit
Press +, choose Armenian, and pick the layout you want
winSteps: Open Settings → Time & language → Language & region
Add a language and choose Armenian
Open its options and add the Armenian keyboard

why.heading: Why touch typing is worth it in Armenian specifically
why.body: Hunting for letters keeps your eyes on the keyboard, and in a script you're still learning that means you never read what you're writing. Touch typing frees your attention to go back to the words — which is why it tends to speed up reading and spelling alongside typing speed. Accuracy comes first here: every lesson gates on accuracy rather than speed, because speed built on sloppy fingering has to be unlearned later.

items.text: Ten-finger touch-typing lessons on the Armenian phonetic layout, from the home keys up. Each lesson unlocks when you hit its accuracy target.

items.title: Races

faq.q: Do I need an Armenian keyboard to use this?
faq.a: No. The on-screen keyboard shows every key and highlights the next one, so you can work through the whole course on a Latin keyboard. Adding the system layout (see the steps above) is what lets you type Armenian everywhere else once you're comfortable.

faq.q: Which Armenian keyboard layout does this teach?
faq.a: The Armenian phonetic layout, where letters sit on the keys of the Latin letters they sound like — ա on A, ս on S, դ on D, and so on. It's the easiest starting point if you already type in a Latin alphabet, since most of the home row transfers directly.

faq.q: Is it really free?
faq.a: Yes — the lessons, the typing test and the races are all free, with no account and no ads. Signing in to Haylingua just means your races run under your own name and your results are saved to your profile.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn?
faq.a: Most people get through the home-row lessons in a few sittings and can type simple Armenian words without looking within a week or two of short daily practice. Speed keeps climbing for months after that, but the useful threshold — not hunting for letters — comes quickly.

faq.q: How is typing speed measured?
faq.a: In words per minute, using the standard convention that five characters count as one word, alongside accuracy as a percentage of correct keystrokes. Both are shown live while you type.

about.heading: Hear Armenian the way it's actually spoken
about.p1: Armenian spelling doesn't map onto English letters, and romanization only gets you so far — two words that look nearly identical written out can sound completely different. Hearing a passage read by a native Armenian voice is the fastest way to close that gap, whether you're checking a name, a message from family, or a line of poetry you can read but can't quite pronounce.
about.p2: This reader uses Armenian neural voices trained on Armenian itself, not a foreign voice approximating the sounds. It handles Standard Eastern Armenian, including the letters and punctuation that generic text-to-speech tools usually mangle. Paste anything from a single word to a full paragraph, pick a male or female voice, and share the result as a link.

faq.q: Is the Armenian text-to-speech reader free?
faq.a: Yes. You can use it without an account, up to a daily character allowance shown under the text box. Signing in to Haylingua raises that allowance significantly and lets you read longer passages in one go.

faq.q: Which Armenian does it speak?
faq.a: Standard Eastern Armenian, the variety used in Armenia, in native Armenian neural voices. Western Armenian text will still be read, but with Eastern pronunciation.

faq.q: Why is there a limit?
faq.a: Generating speech costs money per character, so an open-ended free tool would be trivial to abuse. The limits are generous enough for real study and reading, and signing in gives you a much higher ceiling.

faq.q: Can I share what I made?
faq.a: Yes. Copy link puts the text into the URL, so whoever opens it sees the same passage ready to play. Short passages only — up to 400 characters.

faq.q: Can I download the audio?
faq.a: Not from this page yet. Replaying a passage you've already generated is free and instant, so you can loop a sentence as many times as you need while practising.

faq.q: Does it work with Armenian written in Latin letters?
faq.a: No — it needs the Armenian script. Text like "barev dzez" will be read as if it were a foreign word, because that is what it looks like to the voice. If you can't type Armenian yet, our free typing trainer teaches the Armenian keyboard from the home row up.

faq.q: Is my text saved anywhere?
faq.a: The generated audio is cached by content so that identical text isn't paid for twice, and cached files are cleared out after 90 days. Nothing is attached to your account, shown to other people, or used to build a profile of you.

faq.q: Can I use it on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. It runs in any modern mobile browser with no app to install — useful when the Armenian text you need to hear arrived in a message on that same phone.

faq.q: How is this different from Google Translate's audio?
faq.a: General-purpose translation tools treat Armenian as one of a hundred languages and often route it through a voice that isn't native to it. These are Armenian neural voices, and the tool does one thing: read Armenian text properly, with the alphabet and punctuation handled correctly.

useCases.heading: What people use the reader for

items.title: Messages from family
items.text: A relative writes in Armenian and you can make out the letters but not the rhythm. Paste the message and hear where the stress actually falls.

items.title: Names and place names
items.text: Armenian surnames and toponyms are where romanization fails hardest. Hear ղ, խ and ց as they really sound before you say a name out loud.

items.title: Homework and textbooks
items.text: Check your own reading against a native voice line by line, instead of guessing at a passage you have only ever seen written down.

items.title: Poetry and song lyrics
items.text: Armenian verse is built on sound. Hearing Charents or Sayat-Nova read aloud tells you things the printed page cannot.

items.title: Shadowing practice
items.text: Play a sentence, repeat it, play it again. Replays are instant and do not count against your daily allowance.

items.title: Signs, menus and labels
items.text: Type what you saw on a shopfront in Yerevan or on a jar in an Armenian grocery, and find out how it sounds.

how.heading: How the Armenian voice works
how.p1: The reader uses neural text-to-speech voices built for Armenian specifically — hy-AM voices trained on Armenian speech, rather than an English or Russian voice bent into approximating Armenian sounds. That difference is audible immediately on the letters that have no close equivalent in either language.
how.p2: It reads Standard Eastern Armenian, handles the full 39-letter alphabet, and respects Armenian punctuation: the full stop «։», the question mark «՞» and the emphasis mark «՛» all change how a sentence is delivered, the way a comma or a question mark does in English. Text that includes them will be read with the right intonation rather than as a flat string of words.
how.p3: It is not perfect, and it is worth knowing where the edges are. Western Armenian text will be read with Eastern pronunciation, because that is the variety the voices speak. Rare proper nouns, heavy dialect, and words borrowed from other languages mid-sentence can come out approximate. For everyday Armenian — messages, lessons, articles, poetry — it is reliable enough to learn from.

items.title: Work in short passages
items.text: A sentence or two at a time is far more useful than a whole page. You can hold a short passage in your head and repeat it; a long one just washes over you.

items.title: Listen before you read aloud
items.text: Hear the line first, then say it, then hear it again. Reading first locks in whatever pronunciation you already assumed, which is the thing you are trying to correct.

items.title: Try both voices
items.text: The male and female voices differ in pace and pitch. Hearing the same sentence twice, voiced differently, separates what belongs to the language from what belongs to one speaker.

items.title: Keep the Armenian punctuation
items.text: If you are copying text, keep «։» and «՞» rather than swapping in a full stop and a question mark. The Armenian marks are what tell the voice where a sentence ends and whether it is a question.

armenianNameTranslator.disclaimer: This is a phonetic approximation, not an official standard — Armenian has no single fixed way to spell foreign names, the same way a name can be spelled several ways when it moves between any two languages. It follows the sound-based conventions Armenian speakers commonly use for Western names.

faq.q: Is this the official Armenian spelling of my name?
faq.a: No — there's no single official standard for writing foreign names in Armenian. This tool follows the sound-based conventions Armenian speakers commonly use for Western names, but the same name can reasonably be spelled more than one way.

faq.q: Why does the spelling look different from how I say my name?
faq.a: Armenian and English don't share every sound, and English spelling itself doesn't always match pronunciation. The tool works from typical pronunciation patterns, so unusual spellings or nicknames may come out differently than you'd expect.

faq.q: Can I use this for a tattoo or engraving?
faq.a: You can, but we'd recommend double-checking with a native Armenian speaker first — a phonetic guess is a great starting point, not a guarantee, especially for something permanent.

faq.q: Does Armenian have capital and lowercase letters like English?
faq.a: Yes — Armenian has 39 letters, each with its own uppercase and lowercase form. This tool capitalizes the first letter of each name, matching how proper nouns are written in Armenian.

about.heading: Why handwriting still matters for the Armenian alphabet
about.p1: Armenian has 39 letters, and a good number of them are close cousins on the page — ո and օ, ղ and դ, ճ and ձ, ը and ը's neighbours. Reading them apart is one skill; producing them from memory is a different one, and the second is what handwriting builds. Children who only ever tap letters on a screen tend to recognise the alphabet long before they can write it.
about.p2: These worksheets follow the usual tracing pattern: each line starts with three faded letters to trace, then leaves the rest of the line blank so the child forms the letter unaided. The ruled option adds a baseline and a dashed midline, which is what most Armenian schools use to teach consistent letter height. Turn the rules off for older learners who no longer need them.
about.p3: The letters, their order and their romanization come from the same course data Haylingua teaches from, so a child practising here is practising exactly what the lessons use. All 39 letters are included, in the standard modern order — with ՈՒ in position 34 and և at 37.

faq.q: Are the Armenian handwriting worksheets free?
faq.a: Yes, completely. There is no signup, no watermark, and no limit on how many you generate or print. Teachers are welcome to print class sets.

faq.q: How do I save them as a PDF?
faq.a: Press Print, then in the print dialog change the destination to "Save as PDF" (Chrome, Edge) or use the PDF button (Safari, Firefox). You get the same file a PDF download would give you.

faq.q: Can I print just a few letters?
faq.a: Yes. Pick a range — 1–10, 11–20, 21–30, 31–39 — or just the vowels or consonants. One letter set per sheet keeps it manageable for young children.

faq.q: Which Armenian alphabet is this?
faq.a: The modern Eastern Armenian alphabet, all 39 letters in standard order, matching what is taught in Armenia. Western Armenian uses the same letters, so the worksheets work for both — only the pronunciation of some letters differs.

faq.q: What are the guide lines for?
faq.a: The solid baseline and dashed midline help a child keep letters at a consistent height and sitting on the line, which is the hardest part of early handwriting. Switch to Plain once that is no longer a problem.

faq.q: Can I use these in my Armenian school or class?
faq.a: Please do. They are free to print and hand out for any educational use, at home or in a classroom. A link back to the page is appreciated but not required.

meta.title: Armenian Keyboard: How to Type in Armenian on Any Device
meta.description: Add an Armenian keyboard to iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows, ChromeOS or Linux in a few taps — and pick the right layout. Free step-by-step guide, no download needed.

hero.heading: How to type in Armenian on any device
hero.subtext: Every device you already own can type Armenian. There is nothing to download — the keyboard is built in, you just have to switch it on.
hero.note: The harder part is choosing the right layout, so that section is below the steps.

ios.name: iPhone & iPad
ios.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on iPhone or iPad
steps: Open Settings.
Tap General, then Keyboard.
Tap Keyboards, then Add New Keyboard…
Under Other iPhone Keyboards, scroll to Armenian and tap it.
That's it — Armenian is now in your keyboard list.
ios.switch: Tap and hold the globe key at the bottom of the keyboard, then choose Armenian. A quick tap cycles through your keyboards.
ios.caveat: iOS gives you a single Armenian layout with no variant to choose, so there is no wrong choice to make here.

android.name: Android
android.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on Android
steps: Open Settings and find your keyboard settings — on most phones this is System, then Languages & input, then On-screen keyboard.
Tap Gboard (or whichever keyboard app you use).
Tap Languages, then Add keyboard.
Search for Armenian, select it, and choose a layout when prompted.
Tap Done to save it.
android.switch: Tap the globe key on the keyboard to cycle between languages, or hold it to pick one from a list.
android.caveat: Android menus vary quite a bit by manufacturer — Samsung, Xiaomi and others rename these screens. If the path above doesn't match, search your Settings for "keyboard" or "languages".

macos.name: Mac
macos.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on a Mac
steps: Open System Settings (System Preferences on macOS 12 and earlier).
Go to Keyboard.
Next to Text Input, click Edit… (on older versions, open the Input Sources tab).
Click the + button at the bottom left, select Armenian in the list, then pick a layout — see the layout section below.
Click Add, and tick "Show Input menu in menu bar" if you want the flag icon.
macos.switch: Press Control + Space to move to the next input source, or click the flag in the menu bar and choose Armenian.
macos.caveat: macOS offers exactly two Armenian layouts — "Armenian — HM QWERTY" and "Armenian — Western QWERTY". Neither is called "phonetic", which trips people up; HM QWERTY is the one you want for Eastern Armenian.

windows.name: Windows
windows.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on Windows
steps: Open Settings, then Time & language.
Go to Language & region (on Windows 10: Language).
Click Add a language, search for Armenian, and install it.
Click the three dots next to Armenian, choose Language options, then Add a keyboard.
Pick Armenian Phonetic or Armenian Typewriter — see the layout section below.
windows.switch: Press Windows key + Space to cycle through keyboards, or click the language code (ENG / ARM) in the taskbar.
windows.caveat: Windows lists several variants, including Eastern and Western. "Armenian Phonetic" is the QWERTY-based one most learners want.

chromeos.name: ChromeOS
chromeos.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on a Chromebook
steps: Open Settings, then Advanced, then Languages and inputs.
Click Inputs, then Add input methods.
Search for Armenian and tick Armenian Phonetic.
Click Add to save it.
chromeos.switch: Press Ctrl + Shift + Space to switch input methods, or click the input indicator in the status area.
chromeos.caveat: ChromeOS labels its layout "Armenian Phonetic", which is the QWERTY-based mapping shown further down this page.

linux.name: Linux
linux.title: Add the Armenian keyboard on Linux
steps: Open Settings, then Keyboard (GNOME) or Region & Language on older releases.
Under Input Sources, click the + button.
Search for Armenian and choose a variant — Phonetic is the QWERTY-based one.
Click Add.
linux.switch: Press Super + Space on GNOME, or use the input indicator in the top bar. Other desktops differ.
linux.caveat: Paths differ by desktop environment. On KDE the equivalent lives in System Settings, then Input Devices, then Keyboard, then Layouts.

layouts.heading: Which Armenian layout should you choose?
layouts.intro: This is the step people get wrong, and it matters more than the setup itself: the layouts share almost no keys, so switching later means learning to type again from scratch. The operating systems also don't agree on what to call them, which makes the choice harder than it should be.

items.name: Phonetic
items.aka: macOS: HM QWERTY · Windows/ChromeOS: Armenian Phonetic
items.text: Each Armenian letter sits on the Latin key that sounds like it — A gives ա, S gives ս, D gives դ. If you already touch-type in English, most of your muscle memory carries straight over. This is the layout most learners and most of the diaspora use.

items.name: Typewriter
items.aka: Windows: Armenian Typewriter · also called Standard
items.text: The traditional layout inherited from Armenian typewriters, arranged for typing speed in Armenian rather than for similarity to QWERTY. It's common among professional typists in Armenia. Nothing is where an English typist expects it, so it's a much steeper start.

items.name: Western
items.text: A phonetic-style layout adjusted for Western Armenian pronunciation, where several letters correspond to different sounds. Choose it if you are learning or writing Western Armenian; otherwise it will fight you.

layouts.recommendation: If you are unsure: choose Phonetic — HM QWERTY on a Mac, Armenian Phonetic on Windows, ChromeOS and Linux. It's the layout our free typing trainer teaches, and the one most Armenian speakers outside Armenia actually use.

map.heading: The Armenian phonetic layout, key by key
map.text: Here is what the phonetic layout puts under each key. The small Latin letter is the key you press; the large Armenian letter is what appears. Notice how many are near-homophones of the English key — which is exactly why this layout is quick to pick up.
map.caption: A dot means the key isn't part of the letter set our typing lessons teach yet.

faq.q: Do I need to download an Armenian keyboard?
faq.a: No. Every major operating system already includes Armenian — iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows, ChromeOS and Linux all ship it. You are switching on something you already have, not installing anything, so be wary of sites offering an "Armenian keyboard download".

faq.q: Is there an Armenian keyboard app I should install instead?
faq.a: You almost certainly don't need one. The built-in keyboards handle Armenian properly and don't ask for the sweeping permissions that third-party keyboard apps do — a keyboard app can see everything you type, including passwords, so it's a poor trade for something your device does already.

faq.q: What's the difference between phonetic and typewriter layouts?
faq.a: Phonetic maps Armenian letters onto the Latin keys that sound like them, so an English typist can start immediately. Typewriter uses the traditional Armenian arrangement, which is faster once mastered but shares nothing with QWERTY. Most learners should choose phonetic.

faq.q: How do I type the Armenian question mark and other marks?
faq.a: Armenian uses its own punctuation — «։» ends a sentence, «՞» marks a question and «՛» marks emphasis, and they sit above the vowel rather than at the end of the sentence. All of them are on the Armenian keyboard once it's enabled; the exact keys vary by layout.

faq.q: Can I type Armenian without adding a keyboard at all?
faq.a: For a word or two, yes — you can copy characters from our alphabet page. For anything longer it's worth the two minutes to switch the real keyboard on, since copying character by character gets old fast.

faq.q: Why doesn't my Armenian text show up correctly?
faq.a: That's a font problem rather than a keyboard one. The text is fine; the app you're viewing it in has no Armenian-capable font and is drawing boxes instead. Modern phones and browsers include one, so it usually only shows up in older software or unusual apps.
